title: How the Old Testament books were written
categoryTitle: How the Bible came to us
turn: what each book says of itself
premise: Most Old Testament books do not sign their names. A few say plainly who spoke or wrote. Many carry a note from a later hand. For two centuries scholars have built theories of how the books were put together. This study puts each book's own witness first, then the evidence of editing, then the theories in their holders' own words, and keeps the three apart.
question: What does a book say about how it was made, and how far can anyone reason beyond that?
outcomes: Find what a book says about its own writer, and tell it apart from what tradition said later.
Name the signs of a later hand in the five books of Moses, and say what each sign shows and what it does not.
Describe the documentary hypothesis as its holders state it, and give the evangelical answer from the evidence.
Set out the case for one Isaiah and for several, and for an early and a late Daniel, with who holds each view.
Say who “Darius the Mede” may have been, and why no answer is settled yet.
Look up any Old Testament book's writer, date and setting in one line, and see where views differ.

boundaries.in: The making of the Old Testament books. The five books of Moses: what they say of Moses' writing, the signs of later editing, the documentary hypothesis and the answer to it. Isaiah and Daniel: the evidence and the views. Who Darius the Mede was. A one-line reference for all thirty-nine books.
out: Which books belong to the Old Testament, and when the list closed: How the canon took shape.

How the words were copied, and how one reading is weighed against another (the Masoretes, the Greek Old Testament, Jeremiah's two forms): The text of the Bible. The scrolls themselves: The Dead Sea Scrolls.
The date of the exodus, and so of Moses: Israel from the exodus to Solomon. This page chooses neither date.

Daniel 8 and 11 set beside the record of the Greek kings, and the readings of Daniel 11:36–45: Between the Testaments. The seventy weeks and the order of end-time events: theology's Daniel and Revelation.
Isaiah's passage about Cyrus read in its setting, and Cyrus himself: The return from exile.

What each kind of writing asks of a reader: theology's The kinds of writing in the Bible. How Hebrew poems and stories are built: Hebrew poetry and biblical narrative. The Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra: How Hebrew works.
Whether Genesis copied Babylonian stories, and Proverbs beside Egyptian wisdom: The Bible and the ancient Near East.
The New Testament books: How the New Testament books were written. Crawford Toy (1879) and the Baptist debates over Scripture: Baptist history.
What Scripture teaches about its own inspiration and truth: theology's Scripture (the word of God). This page reports evidence; it does not argue that doctrine.

stance.head: What this site holds
stance.confessionSource: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article I (the Scriptures)
stance.body: The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 says Scripture has “God for its author” and is “truth, without any mixture of error” (article I). It also confesses that God's knowledge reaches all things, the future included (article II). It does not list who wrote each book. So this page holds three things in the site's own voice. What a book says of itself is true. A prophecy that names a king or a kingdom before it comes is possible, because God knows the future. A theory that needs a book's own claims to be false is described as others' view, in its holders' words, and is never adopted.
stance.open: Where scholars who hold Scripture true differ, this page shows each view with the people who hold it, and does not choose. That covers how much of the five books Moses wrote himself and how much is later inspired editing, who Darius the Mede was, and when Job, Joel or Obadiah was written. The page also keeps two points in view. A later note in a book does not make the book's claims false. A theory with many holders does not become evidence by having them.

pentateuch.headline: Moses wrote. Someone wrote his death.
pentateuch.lead: In Jewish terms these five books are the Torah, the teaching. They are the first of the three parts of the Hebrew Bible, {{check:c1}}read through in the synagogue in weekly portions, today usually over one year, though an older three-year cycle from the land of Israel is also recorded{{/check}}. Jewish and Christian tradition both call them the five books of Moses. None of the five says who wrote the whole. What they do say is narrower, and more exact.

selfWitness.says: After the battle with Amalek, the LORD tells Moses to write it in a book as a memorial.
Moses writes down all the LORD's words, and then reads the Book of the Covenant to the people (24:7).
The LORD tells Moses to write down the words of the renewed covenant.
At the LORD's command, Moses records the stages of Israel's journey.
Moses writes down this law and gives it to the priests.
Moses writes down the song of chapter 32 and teaches it to Israel.
Moses finishes writing the words of this law in a book, and has it placed beside the ark (31:26).

pentateuch.selfNote: These verses say Moses wrote laws, a battle record, a list of journeys, a song and the book of Deuteronomy's law. None of them claims Genesis for him, and none says who set down the whole. The case for Moses as the writer of all five rests also on how the rest of Scripture speaks of them.

remembered.says: Joshua builds an altar as the Book of the Law of Moses directs, and writes a copy of the law of Moses on stones.
King Amaziah spares his father's murderers' children, following what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses. The law he follows is Deuteronomy 24:16.
After the exile, the priests serve according to the book of Moses, and that book is read aloud to the people.
Jesus asks the Sadducees whether they have not read, in the book of Moses, the passage about the bush. That passage is Exodus 3.
Jesus says Moses wrote about him, and sets Moses' writings beside his own words.
Jesus names the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms as Scripture that speaks of him.

remembered.where: Josephus, Against Apion 1.8 (late first century AD)
remembered.says: Josephus counts twenty-two sacred books, five of them Moses', which hold the laws and the history down to Moses' death.

In a teaching older than the Talmud itself, Moses wrote his own book. {{check:c2}}Rabbi Judah (some say Rabbi Nehemiah) says Joshua wrote the Torah's last eight verses, the account of Moses' death. Rabbi Simeon says Moses wrote even those, as God spoke them, in tears{{/check}}.

pentateuch.rememberedNote: From Joshua to Jesus, the Law is the law of Moses and the book is the book of Moses. The Jewish teachers who held this most firmly were also the first to say that Joshua may have written the end.

laterHand.head: His death
laterHand.evidence: The last chapter tells of Moses' death and burial in Moab, Israel's thirty days of mourning, and Joshua leading after him.
laterHand.inference: These verses were written after Moses died. Almost every reader, ancient and modern, has said so. The Talmud gives them to Joshua.
laterHand.limit: This shows a later hand at the end of the book. It does not show how much of the rest is later.

laterHand.head: Looking back
laterHand.evidence: The place of Moses' grave is said to be still unknown in the writer's day. No prophet like Moses is said to have arisen since.
laterHand.inference: The writer looks back across some span of time.
laterHand.limit: The text does not say how long the span was. Readers place this writer anywhere from Joshua's generation to the time of the kings or later.

laterHand.head: A new name for an old place
laterHand.evidence: Abram chases the raiders as far as Dan. Judges says the city was called Laish until the tribe of Dan took it and renamed it.
laterHand.inference: The place name in Genesis has been brought up to date for later readers, as a history book today might speak of New York in the days when it was New Amsterdam.
laterHand.limit: Some readers think an older, different Dan is meant. Either way, the change touches a place name and not the account.

laterHand.head: Before any king
laterHand.evidence: A list of Edom's kings is introduced as kings who reigned before any king reigned over the Israelites.
laterHand.inference: Many readers take this as written after Israel had kings. {{check:c3}}Others, among them C. F. Keil in the Keil and Delitzsch commentary, read it in the light of God's promise to Jacob that kings would come from him (Genesis 35:11), and of Moses' own law of the king (Deuteronomy 17:14–20){{/check}}.
laterHand.limit: The verse can be read both ways. On its own it cannot fix a date.

laterHand.head: Then in the land
laterHand.evidence: When Abram arrives, the narrator notes that the Canaanites were in the land at that time.
laterHand.inference: Thomas Hobbes (1651) and Baruch Spinoza (1670) read this as written after the Canaanites were gone.
laterHand.limit: The note may simply say that the promised land was already occupied, which is where the passage goes next (12:7). This is a reading of one phrase, not a measurement.

laterHand.head: Praise of the writer
laterHand.evidence: Moses is called more humble than anyone on the face of the earth.
laterHand.inference: Some readers take this as an inspired note added later. Others take it as Moses' own plain statement of fact, written as a prophet records what is true, even about himself.
laterHand.limit: Neither reading changes what the verse says about Moses.

laterHand.head: A book quoted
laterHand.evidence: The text quotes a few lines from a book it names, the Book of the Wars of the LORD.
laterHand.inference: The writer used at least one earlier written source, and said so.
laterHand.limit: Using a source fits a writer in Moses' day as well as a later one. The source itself is lost.

laterHand.head: Moses as “he”
laterHand.evidence: Outside the speeches of Deuteronomy, where Moses says “I”, the books speak of Moses in the third person.
laterHand.inference: Critics have taken this as a sign of a second writer. Gleason Archer and K. A. Kitchen answer that ancient writers did write of themselves in the third person. Julius Caesar's account of his wars in Gaul is the usual example.
laterHand.limit: The third person fits a writer speaking of himself or someone else speaking of him. By itself it decides nothing.

views.name: Moses wrote the five books, apart from a few later notes
views.held: William Henry Green (1895), Oswald T. Allis (1943), Edward J. Young (1949) and Gleason Archer (1964), in their introductions and studies; and, in its own terms, the teaching in Bava Batra that gives Joshua the last eight verses.
views.reading: Moses is the writer of the whole as it stands. The exceptions are the account of his death and a small number of updated names and notes, added soon after by an inspired hand.

views.name: Moses is the author and the source, and later inspired editing may go further than a few notes
views.held: John Sailhamer, The Meaning of the Pentateuch (2009), {{check:c4}}argued for a later prophetic shaping of Moses' work{{/check}}. {{check:c5}}Other evangelical Old Testament scholars, among them Bruce Waltke, Genesis (2001), and Raymond Dillard and Tremper Longman, An Introduction to the Old Testament (1994), allow updating across the books{{/check}}.
views.reading: The substance and the authority are Moses'. The final form may come from inspired editors, much as Proverbs openly says that some of its sayings were “copied by the men of Hezekiah” (Proverbs 25:1 · BSB).

views.name: Moses drew on older records for Genesis
views.held: P. J. Wiseman, New Discoveries in Babylonia about Genesis (1936); {{check:c6}}R. K. Harrison, Introduction to the Old Testament (1969){{/check}}; Duane Garrett, Rethinking Genesis (1991).
views.reading: Genesis repeats a Hebrew heading, toledot, usually translated “account” or “generations”. On this view the heading marks older family records that Moses gathered. The view is about what Moses used, so it can sit with either of the two views above.

pentateuch.chicago: The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978), signed by evangelical scholars of many churches, draws its line in article XVIII. {{check:c7}}It calls for reading the text by grammatico-historical exegesis, and denies the legitimacy of any treatment of the text or quest for sources lying behind it that leads to relativizing, dehistoricizing or discounting its teaching, or “rejecting its claims to authorship”{{/check}}. Both views above stay inside that line.
pentateuch.stand: This site holds, with the rest of Scripture and with Jesus, that the Law is Moses' (Mark 12:26; John 5:46–47). Between the first two views, both held by scholars who hold Scripture true, it does not choose. The third can sit with either. On every one of these views, what the books say of themselves stands.

documentary.headline: Four sources. No document found.
documentary.lead: The documentary hypothesis holds that the five books were woven together from four written sources. On this theory the sources came from different centuries and none of them is by Moses. The theory took its classic form in Julius Wellhausen's history of Israel of 1878. It is described here in its holders' terms, and then the answer is given. It is not a view this site holds.

sources.name: The Yahwist
sources.theyHold: Uses the LORD's name (German Jahwe) from the beginning. Vivid stories, with God described in human terms. Linked with Judah.
sources.date: Usually given as about 950 to 850 BC

sources.name: The Elohist
sources.theyHold: Calls God Elohim until the name is revealed in Exodus. Linked with the northern kingdom.
sources.date: Usually given as about 850 to 750 BC

sources.name: Deuteronomy
sources.theyHold: Identified with the book of the law found in the temple in King Josiah's day (2 Kings 22).

sources.name: The Priestly source
sources.theyHold: Genealogies, dates, the tabernacle and the laws of sacrifice. Written by priests during or after the exile.
sources.date: Usually given as about 550 to 450 BC, with a final editor after it

documentary.datesNote: These dates are the ones textbook summaries usually give. {{check:c8}}Holders have never agreed on them exactly{{/check}}.

history.what: {{check:c9}}A Jewish commentator who hints, on Deuteronomy 1:1, that a few verses may come from after Moses{{/check}}.
Leviathan, chapter 33. From Deuteronomy 34 and Genesis 12:6, he argues that the books were written later than Moses, though Moses wrote what the text says he wrote.
Theological-Political Treatise, chapter 8. He argues that the five books were written long after Moses.
A French physician. He proposes that Moses himself used older sources for Genesis, marked by the two names for God. The first source theory was offered in defence of Moses.
{{check:c10}}His introduction to the Old Testament (three volumes, 1780–1783) carries source division further{{/check}}.
Divides the material that uses Elohim into two sources.
Argues that the priestly law is the latest layer, not the earliest.
Articles on how the first books were composed, then Geschichte Israels, volume 1 (1878). It was retitled Prolegomena to the History of Israel in 1883 and published in English in 1885.
His Introduction to the Literature of the Old Testament brings the scheme to English readers.

history.who: John Van Seters, Rolf Rendtorff, R. N. Whybray
history.what: Critical scholars who in different ways question the four separate documents. Whybray's The Making of the Pentateuch (1987) doubts the sources can be found at all.
The Composition of the Pentateuch restates a four-source model, now called neo-documentary.

wellhausen.quote: “in the summer of 1867, I learned through Ritschl that Karl Heinrich Graf placed the Law later than the Prophets, and, almost without knowing his reasons for the hypothesis, I was prepared to accept it; I readily acknowledged to myself the possibility of understanding Hebrew antiquity without the book of the Torah.”
wellhausen.source: {{check:c11}}Julius Wellhausen, Prolegomena to the History of Israel (English 1885), Introduction{{/check}}
wellhausen.note: Read what he says he did. He was ready to accept Graf's order before he knew Graf's reasons, and then built the history that supported it. The order was the heart of the theory: the prophets first, then the law. On that view the priestly law, which the books place at Sinai, belongs to the time after the exile.

criteria.head: Two names for God
criteria.theyHold: Before Exodus, one strand calls God Elohim and another uses the LORD's name. In Exodus 6:3 God tells Moses that the patriarchs did not know him by his name the LORD. Holders read that verse as the point where one source first learns the name.
criteria.answer: Umberto Cassuto, a Jewish scholar in Italy and later Jerusalem, and not an evangelical, argued that the names are chosen for their meaning: God as Creator over all, and the LORD as Israel's covenant God. Alec Motyer (1959) read Exodus 6:3 as being about knowing what the name means, not hearing it for the first time. Genesis itself has Abram calling on the LORD's name (Genesis 12:8).
criteria.limit: Counts of the names follow the standard Hebrew text. Ancient copies and translations do not always agree on which name stands in a verse, {{check:c12}}and critics of the theory, among them Johannes Dahse (from 1903, at length in 1912) and Harold Wiener, have used that against it{{/check}}.

criteria.head: Stories told twice
criteria.theyHold: Several stories are told twice: a patriarch passing off his wife as his sister (Genesis 12:10–20; 20; 26:1–11), and creation (Genesis 1:1–2:3 and 2:4–25). Holders also see two strands mixed together in the flood.
criteria.answer: Kitchen and Garrett point out that repetition is a known feature of ancient Near Eastern writing. Genesis 1 and 2 answer different questions: how the world was made, and how the man and woman came to be in the garden. The wife-sister stories involve different people, places and outcomes.
criteria.limit: Seeing a pattern does not prove one writer, and splitting a pattern does not prove two. On both sides, the test can assume what it sets out to show.

criteria.head: Vocabulary and style
criteria.theyHold: Each source has its own words and manner, such as the Priestly source's lists and dates.
criteria.answer: A change of subject changes style. Any author writes a genealogy or a law code differently from a story. Whybray, who was not an evangelical, judged that the tests for sources could not bear the weight put on them.
criteria.limit: The differences in style are real. What they show is disputed.

criteria.head: One altar or many
criteria.theyHold: This was Wellhausen's central argument. The patriarchs and early Israel offer sacrifice in many places. Deuteronomy requires one chosen place (Deuteronomy 12). The priestly law assumes that one place already exists. So Deuteronomy belongs with Josiah, and the priestly law after the exile.
criteria.answer: Meredith Kline, Treaty of the Great King (1963), and Kitchen compared the shape of Deuteronomy with treaties from the second millennium BC. The law of one place looks ahead to a place the LORD will choose and does not name it. Samuel's later altars came after the sanctuary at Shiloh was lost (1 Samuel 4; 7:9; Jeremiah 7:12).
criteria.limit: {{check:c13}}Scholars disagree on whether Deuteronomy's form fits treaties of the second millennium better, as Kitchen holds, or of the first, as Moshe Weinfeld, Deuteronomy and the Deuteronomic School (1972), argued{{/check}}.

documentary.afterWellhausen: The theory is not one settled result. Since the 1970s many critical scholars have given up four continuous documents for fragments, layers or a single later composition. Others defend the four sources again. This study infers that the claim “scholars agree” describes no actual agreement. The limit runs the other way too: that critics disagree does not by itself prove that Moses wrote the books.

answer.head: The evangelical answer
points: No copy of J, E, D or P has ever been found. {{check:c14}}Every ancient witness to these books, from the Qumran scrolls to the Samaritan Pentateuch, has the five books much as we read them, with differences only of wording and detail{{/check}}.

The tests used to divide the text (the names, the repeated stories, the styles) each have an explanation inside one composition, as Green (1895), Allis (1943), Cassuto (English 1961) and Kitchen (2003) argued, each from his own evidence.
The rest of Scripture, and Jesus, speak of the Law as Moses' (Mark 12:26; John 5:46–47). What Scripture teaches about itself is set out in theology's Scripture (the word of God), not argued here.
answer.limit: Moses' own copy does not survive either. Both sides argue from the text as we have it.

documentary.stand: This site holds that the five books are Moses' and true. The documentary hypothesis is reported as a reconstruction that scholars have held, in their own words. It is not a correction of the text, and the site does not adopt it, because it requires the books' own account of Moses' writing to be mistaken.

isaiah.headline: One scroll. Two halves?
isaiah.lead: The book is headed as the vision of “Isaiah son of Amoz” (Isaiah 1:1 · BSB) in the reigns of Uzziah to Hezekiah, roughly 740 to 700 BC. From chapter 40 on, it speaks comfort to a people in exile and names Cyrus, the Persian king who let the exiles go home. Cyrus came to power more than a century after Isaiah lived.

lines.quote: confirms the message of His servant
lines.note: The LORD sets his foretelling against the idols. The prediction is part of the book's own argument.

lines.quote: My shepherd will fulfill all that I desire
lines.note: Said of Cyrus, with his task named: Jerusalem rebuilt.
A king set apart for a task, as Saul and David were. It does not make Cyrus the Messiah.

lines.quote: though you have not known Me
lines.note: The LORD names and uses a king who does not worship him.

evidence.head: The Great Isaiah Scroll
evidence.evidence: {{check:c15}}The complete Isaiah scroll from Qumran Cave 1 (1QIsaᵃ) is usually dated to about 150 to 100 BC, often to about 125 BC{{/check}}. It runs all sixty-six chapters as one book. It has no title or break marking a new book at chapter 40. {{check:c16}}The scribe left a gap of about three lines after chapter 33, at the foot of a column, which W. H. Brownlee read as the midpoint of one book laid out in two matching halves, not the start of a second book{{/check}}.
evidence.inference: By the second century BC the book was copied, read and received as one book under one name.
evidence.limit: A scroll shows how a book was received when it was copied. It cannot show how many hands wrote it centuries before.

evidence.head: Ben Sira, about 180 BC
evidence.evidence: Ben Sira (Sirach 48:22–25) praises Isaiah in Hezekiah's day as the prophet who saw the last things and comforted those who mourned in Zion. That is the language of chapters 40 and 61.
evidence.inference: A Jewish teacher of the early second century BC gave the comfort of the book's second half to Isaiah of Hezekiah's court.
evidence.limit: This is how one ancient reader received the book, not a report of how it was written.

evidence.head: How the New Testament quotes it
evidence.evidence: Matthew 3:3 quotes Isaiah 40:3 under Isaiah's name. John 12:38–41 quotes Isaiah 53:1 and 6:10 one after the other, both as Isaiah's, and says Isaiah saw Christ's glory. Romans 10:16 and 10:20 quote Isaiah 53:1 and 65:1 as words Isaiah spoke.
evidence.inference: The apostles cite both halves of the book under one prophet's name, and John joins the two halves in one breath.
evidence.limit: Scholars who divide the book answer that these quotations name the book, not its writer. Evangelical scholars reply that John 12:41 speaks of a person who saw.

evidence.head: The case for later hands
evidence.evidence: Chapters 40 to 66 address people in Babylon and Jerusalem in ruins (44:26; 64:10–11) and name Cyrus. Their style and themes differ from chapters 1 to 39. {{check:c17}}Johann Christoph Döderlein (1775) and Eichhorn (in the 1780s) argued for a second writer{{/check}}. Bernhard Duhm (1892) set chapters 56 to 66 apart as a third.
evidence.inference: The argument rests partly on the change of setting and style, and partly on the premise that a prophet speaks only to his own day.
evidence.limit: The book presents the later setting as foreseen (44:26; 45:4). The style argument has been answered by those who note shared phrases across both halves, such as the Holy One of Israel.

views.name: Isaiah of Jerusalem wrote the whole book
views.held: Jewish and Christian readers through most of history, and Josephus. Oswald T. Allis, The Unity of Isaiah (1950); Edward J. Young, Who Wrote Isaiah? (1958); Alec Motyer, The Prophecy of Isaiah (1993); John Oswalt, The Book of Isaiah, chapters 40–66 (1998). Most conservative evangelical and Southern Baptist scholars.
views.reading: Naming Cyrus in advance is prediction, and the book presents it that way.

views.name: Two or three writers
views.held: The majority among academic biblical scholars since the late 1700s: Duhm (1892); Claus Westermann; Joseph Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 40–55 (2002).
views.reading: Chapters 40 to 55 come from an unnamed prophet among the exiles in the 540s BC, and 56 to 66 from the time after the return.

views.name: Many hands, one designed book
views.held: Some critical scholars, among them Brevard Childs, Isaiah (2001), and H. G. M. Williamson, The Book Called Isaiah (1994).
views.reading: The book is read as a deliberate whole, while still being held to come from more than one writer.

isaiah.stand: The site's own voice holds that God's knowledge reaches the future, so a prophecy that names a king in advance is no difficulty. The site reads the book under the name Scripture gives it. A second or third Isaiah is reported as others' reconstruction, not as a correction of the text. The Cyrus passage in its setting belongs to The return from exile; theology's Isaiah teaches the book.
isaiah.note: This page does not read Isaiah 52:13–53:12. Where that passage is read, the Jewish reading of the servant is given first, in the study that owns it: theology's Christ in the Old Testament.

daniel.headline: Exact prophecy. Disputed date.
daniel.lead: The book is set in Babylon, from the third year of King Jehoiakim to “the third year of Cyrus king of Persia” (Daniel 10:1 · BSB). The stories in chapters 1 to 6 speak of Daniel as “he”. The visions in chapters 7 to 12 are in his own first person (7:2; 8:1; 9:2; 10:2). It is written in two languages: Hebrew in 1:1–2:4, Aramaic from 2:4 to 7:28, and Hebrew again to the end.

named.quote: The two-horned ram that you saw represents the kings of Media and Persia.
The shaggy goat represents the king of Greece, and the large horn between his eyes is the first king.
Three more kings will arise in Persia, and then a fourth, who will be far richer than all the others. By the power of his wealth, he will stir up everyone against the kingdom of Greece.

daniel.namedNote: The book names kingdoms and counts kings, but names no Greek king. Setting Daniel 11:3–35 beside the record of the years from 330 to 164 BC is the work of Between the Testaments. That study shows how closely the two run.

evidence.head: Copies at Qumran
evidence.evidence: {{check:c18}}Fragments of eight copies of Daniel were found in the Qumran caves{{/check}}. {{check:c19}}One text there, the Florilegium (4Q174), cites “the book of Daniel the prophet”{{/check}}. A radiocarbon study published in 2025 dated one copy of Daniel 8 to 11 (4Q114) to between 230 and 160 BC.
evidence.inference: If that range holds, very little time is left between a writing in the 160s and a copy of it. Some take this to make a date after 164 BC very hard.
evidence.limit: The radiocarbon study was read only through reports of it, and its range overlaps the 160s. The question of when the book was written is not closed by it.

evidence.head: Early readers
evidence.evidence: 1 Maccabees, written about 100 BC, holds up Daniel's friends and Daniel as examples (2:59–60). Josephus says the nation suffered under Antiochus Epiphanes as Daniel had written many years before (Antiquities 10.11.7). Jesus speaks of “the abomination of desolation,” described by the prophet Daniel (Matthew 24:15 · BSB).
evidence.inference: Within two or three centuries, Jewish readers and then Jesus received Daniel as a prophet and his book as written before the events.
evidence.limit: Reception is not itself a date of writing. It is the earliest testimony there is.

evidence.head: Belshazzar
evidence.evidence: Belshazzar was once known only from Daniel. A cylinder of Nabonidus found at Ur names Belshazzar as his eldest son. {{check:c20}}A Babylonian text, the Verse Account of Nabonidus, says Nabonidus entrusted the kingship to his eldest son when he went away to Tema in Arabia{{/check}}. In Daniel 5:16, Belshazzar offers to make Daniel third in the kingdom.
evidence.inference: The book knows a detail of the last Babylonian court that later writers such as Herodotus did not record.
evidence.limit: It shows the writer had sound information about that court. It does not by itself fix the date of writing.

evidence.head: The words used
evidence.evidence: Daniel 3 names musical instruments with a few Greek words. The book also has Persian loanwords. Those who date it late have argued that the Hebrew and Aramaic fit a late date. K. A. Kitchen's study of the Aramaic (1965) answered that it fits the earlier period as well.
evidence.inference: Greek instruments could travel before Greek rule, and Persian words suit a writer who lived under Persia.
evidence.limit: Arguments from language have been made in both directions, and neither side regards them as settling the question by themselves.

views.name: In the sixth century BC, as the book presents itself
views.held: Jewish and Christian tradition; Josephus; Jerome and Calvin; conservative scholars, among them Edward J. Young, The Prophecy of Daniel (1949), Joyce Baldwin (Tyndale commentary, 1978), and {{check:c21}}Stephen R. Miller in the New American Commentary (1994), published by the Southern Baptist publisher{{/check}}.
views.forIt: The book places its visions in the reigns of Belshazzar, Darius and Cyrus (8:1; 9:1; 10:1). God “removes kings and establishes them” (Daniel 2:21 · BSB) and knows the future, so a prophecy this exact is what such a God could give. Jesus calls Daniel a prophet. The Qumran copies and 1 Maccabees come early.
views.against: Those who hold the later date answer that the detail grows sharper as it nears 167 BC and becomes looser after that.

views.name: About 167 to 164 BC, under Antiochus IV
views.held: Porphyry, in the third century AD, known through Jerome. Most modern critical scholars, among them John J. Collins in the Hermeneia commentary (1993). Many of them hold that the stories in chapters 1 to 6 are older and that the visions were written during the crisis.
views.forIt: On this view the visions know of the plundered temple, its desecration and the resistance, but not the rededication of 164 BC or how Antiochus died. In the Hebrew Bible, Daniel stands among the Writings, not among the Prophets.
views.against: The view rests on the premise that the writer could not know the future, and the book itself denies that premise. The arguments from language have been answered. The radiocarbon date leaves little time between writing and copying.

daniel.stand: In the site's own voice, Daniel is Scripture, “truth, without any mixture of error”, and God's knowledge reaches all things, including the future. So this site reads Daniel as it presents itself: a prophet of the sixth century BC who was shown these kings before they came. The late date is reported as others' reconstruction, not as a correction of the text. The readings of Daniel 11:36–45 belong to Between the Testaments, and the order of end-time events to theology's Daniel and Revelation.
daniel.limit: That Daniel 11 and the record agree shows that the text and the events match. It cannot by itself show when the text was written, because that depends on whether one allows that God foretold it.

darius.headline: One name. Five answers.
darius.question: Daniel says Darius the Mede took the kingdom after Belshazzar died (5:31). He is king in chapter 6, and Daniel prays in his first year (9:1; 11:1). Daniel 9:1 calls him son of Ahasuerus, a Mede by descent. Daniel 6:28 speaks of the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus together. No record outside the Bible has yet been found naming a Darius who ruled Babylon between Nabonidus and Cyrus.
darius.record: {{check:c22}}The Nabonidus Chronicle says Cyrus's army entered Babylon in 539 BC under Ugbaru, governor of Gutium. It says Gubaru, Cyrus's officer, appointed officials in Babylon, and that Ugbaru died a few weeks later{{/check}}.

views.name: Gubaru, the governor
views.held: John C. Whitcomb, Darius the Mede (1959).
views.reading: The governor whom Cyrus set over Babylon, given a throne name.
views.limit: No record calls Gubaru a king, or Darius.

views.name: Cyrus himself
views.held: D. J. Wiseman, in Notes on Some Problems in the Book of Daniel (1965). {{check:c23}}Joyce Baldwin leaned toward this view (1978){{/check}}.
views.reading: Daniel 6:28 is read as the reign of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus. On this view Darius the Mede is Cyrus under another title.
views.limit: The reading needs the Hebrew word for “and” to mean “that is”. Daniel 9:1 gives Darius a father named Ahasuerus, while Cyrus's known father was Cambyses.

views.name: Ugbaru, the general
views.held: {{check:c24}}William H. Shea, in articles in Andrews University Seminary Studies, especially Darius the Mede: An Update (1982){{/check}}.
views.reading: The commander who took the city and briefly ruled it.
views.limit: The chronicle has him die within weeks, which leaves little room for the events of chapter 6.

views.name: Cyaxares II, son of Astyages
views.held: {{check:c25}}Steven D. Anderson, Darius the Mede: A Reappraisal, a doctoral dissertation (Dallas Theological Seminary, 2014){{/check}}. It follows Xenophon's Cyropaedia, and Josephus, Antiquities 10.11.4, which says Darius was the son of Astyages and had another name among the Greeks.
views.reading: A Median king who reigned with Cyrus, Cyrus's uncle in Xenophon's account.
views.limit: Herodotus and the Babylonian records know no Cyaxares II, and Xenophon's book is partly a romance.

views.name: A figure made from mixed memories
views.held: H. H. Rowley, Darius the Mede and the Four World Empires in the Book of Daniel (1935), and most critical scholars.
views.reading: On this view the writer confused the Persian Darius I with a Median kingdom required by a scheme of four kingdoms. This is others' view, and it denies what the text claims.
views.limit: The answer given to it: the book keeps the Mede apart from the Persian kings it names, and the absence of a name in the record is not evidence of absence. Belshazzar was once missing from the record too.

darius.stand: Among the first four answers, all held by scholars who hold the text true, this page does not choose. The fifth is described as others' view. The evidence that would settle it would be a Babylonian or Persian text that names Darius.

table.headline: Thirty-nine books. One line each.
table.lead: Each row gives what the book says about its own writer, the traditional view of who wrote it, the date and setting that view gives, and where scholars who hold Scripture true differ. Theology's book studies link here, not to a second account of their own.
table.order: The rows follow the order of English Bibles. In Jewish terms the same books stand in three parts: the Torah (the five books); the Prophets (the Former Prophets, Joshua to Kings, and the Latter Prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve, counted as one book); and the Writings (Psalms, Proverbs, Job, the five scrolls, Daniel, Ezra–Nehemiah and Chronicles).
table.note: Dates are ranges and come from the traditional view. Where a book's date hangs on the date of the exodus, both are given, and this page chooses neither. Critical datings are not listed row by row. Where one denies what a book says of itself, the row says so in a word and the study's sections give the detail.

claims.claim: “Scholars agree that Moses did not write the Pentateuch.”
claims.head: Many scholars hold it. They do not agree how.
claims.evidence: Critical scholars have divided over four documents, fragments, layers or one late composition since the 1970s. Evangelical scholars from Green to Kitchen hold that Moses is the author.
claims.inference: “Scholars agree” describes no actual agreement, either about what the books are or about when they were written.
claims.limit: A majority within one field is still a fact worth reporting. It is reported here as a majority view, not as evidence.

test.question: A video says “all scholars now know Moses didn't write Genesis.” What should you ask first?

options.text: Which scholars, and what do they think happened instead?
options.why: The answers differ widely, and that disagreement is part of the evidence.

options.text: Nothing; scholars would not say it without proof.
options.why: No source document has been found. The claim rests on reasoning from the text, which can be weighed.

options.text: Whether the video is against the Bible.
options.why: The motive does not change the evidence. Test the claim, not the speaker.

claims.claim: “Believing Moses wrote it means no one else ever touched the text.”
claims.head: The books themselves show another hand at the end.
claims.evidence: Deuteronomy 34 tells of Moses' death. The Talmud, holding firmly to Moses, gives those verses to Joshua.
claims.inference: Holding Moses to be the author has always allowed some later inspired notes. Scholars who hold Scripture true differ over how many.
claims.limit: This does not settle how much editing there is. It shows only that the question is not new and need not frighten anyone.

test.question: Genesis 14:14 says Abram went to Dan, a city named later (Judges 18:29). What does that show?

options.text: That Moses could not have written Genesis.
options.why: An updated place name does not touch the account. It shows a later hand on one word.

options.text: That a later hand updated a name for its readers, or an older Dan is meant.
options.why: Either reading fits what the verse can carry.

options.text: That the story is not historical.
options.why: Updating a name for readers is what a careful history does.

claims.claim: “Scholars found the four sources behind the five books.”
claims.head: They proposed them. No copy has been found.
claims.evidence: J, E, D and P are reconstructed from the text we have. Every ancient copy and translation presents the five books much as we read them.
claims.inference: The hypothesis is a way of explaining features of the text, not a discovery of documents.
claims.limit: A hypothesis can be argued without its documents. The point is only that “found” is the wrong word.

claims.claim: “A prophet could not name Cyrus a century early, so Isaiah 40 to 66 is later.”
claims.head: The argument decides its answer before it begins.
claims.evidence: The book presents the naming as prediction (44:26–28). The Qumran scroll and Ben Sira receive the book as one prophet's.
claims.inference: The late date follows from a premise that God does not foretell. The book's own claim is that he does.
claims.limit: Style and setting are also argued, and they are real features of the text. They are answered in section 03.

claims.claim: “Daniel 11 is too exact to be prophecy.”
claims.head: Exactness shows a match, not a date.
claims.evidence: Daniel 11:3–35 runs close to the record of the Greek kings, as Between the Testaments shows.
claims.inference: The match shows the text and the events agree. Whether it was written before or after depends on whether one allows that God foretold it.
claims.limit: Early copies and early readers bear on the date and are shown in section 04. The match itself does not decide it.

test.question: Daniel 8:21 names “the king of Greece.” What does that let you say?

options.text: That the writer lived after Alexander.
options.why: That follows only if prophecy is ruled out first.

options.text: That the vision names Greece as the kingdom after Persia.
options.why: This is what the verse says. The date of writing is a separate question.

options.text: That the book is not about Greece at all.

confusedWords.note: The author is the one whose work it is. A scribe may write at dictation, as Baruch did for Jeremiah, or copy it later. Moses as author does not require that his hand formed every letter.
A source is anything a writer used. The documentary hypothesis claims four continuous written documents. Using sources (Numbers 21:14) is not the same as being made of documents.
Scholars call an editor a redactor. Proverbs names its editors openly (25:1). An inspired editor adding a note is not a writer of a new book.

confusedWords.word: Anonymous and written under another's name
confusedWords.note: Most Old Testament books are anonymous: they name no writer. That is different from a book claiming a writer who did not write it.

confusedWords.word: The date of the events, of the writing, and of the oldest copy
confusedWords.note: Three different dates. Genesis tells of events long before Moses. A Qumran copy dates the copy, not the writing.
Used by some as a label for chapters 40 to 55, and by others as a name for a supposed separate prophet. A label for a section is not evidence of a person.

reach: Only the five books of Moses, Isaiah and Daniel are argued in full. The other thirty-four books have one line each.

The Bible's own words are read here in the Berean Standard Bible. Where a verse is described rather than quoted, it was not among the texts supplied for this draft and must be quoted from the held text before publishing.
None of the scholarly books named was read for this draft. Their views are given as they are usually reported, and each needs checking against the book before the page goes live.
No Hebrew or Aramaic was compared for this draft.
Nothing on this page can prove who wrote a book. It can show what the book says, what later readers said, and what the evidence of the text can and cannot bear.
